entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.13.3-Job.6.3">Job 13:3-6   3</reference>  But I would speak to the Almighty, <div eID="gen7351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7352" type="x-p"/> And I long to reason with God.   4  And ye however are forgers of lies, <div eID="gen7352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7353" type="x-p"/> Physicians of no value are ye all.   5  Oh that ye would altogether hold your peace, <div eID="gen7353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7354" type="x-p"/> It would be accounted to you as wisdom.   6  Hear now my instruction, <div eID="gen7354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7355" type="x-p"/> Ando hearken to the answers of my lips! <div eID="gen7355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7356" type="x-p"/> He will no longer dispute with the friends; the more they oppose him, the more earnestly he desires to be able to argue his cause before God. אוּלם (<reference osisRef="Job.13.3">Job 13:3</reference>) is disjunctive, like ἀλλά, and introduces a new range of thoughts; lxx ου ̓ μήν δὲ ἀλλά, <hi type="italic">verum enim vero. </hi> True, he has said in Job 9 that no one can maintain his cause before God; but his confidence in God grows in proportion as his distrust of the friends increases; and at the same time, the hope is begotten that God will grant him that softening of the terror of His majesty which he has reserved to himself in connection with this declaration (<reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference>, comp. Job 13:20.). The <hi type="italic">infin. absol.</hi> הוכח, which in <reference osisRef="Job.6.25">Job 6:25</reference> is used almost as a substantive, and indeed as the subject, is here in the place of the object, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.6">Isa 58:6</reference> : to prove, i.e., my cause, to God (אל־אל, like <reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>, אל־פּניו) I long. With ואוּלם (<reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>) the antithesis is introduced anew: I will turn to God, you on the contrary (καὶ ὑμεῖς δὲ). Since the verb טפל, from its primary meaning to spread on, smear on (whence e.g., Talmudic טפלה, the act of throwing on, as when plastering up the cracks of an oven), cogn. תּפל (whence תּפל, plaster, and perhaps also in the signification tasteless, <reference osisRef="Job.6.6">Job 6:6</reference> = sticky, greasy, slimy), does not signify, at least not at first, <hi type="italic">consuere</hi>, but <hi type="italic">assuere</hi> (without any relation of root with תּפר), we explain, not with Olshausen and others, <hi type="italic">concinnatores mendacii,</hi> such as sew together lies as patchwork; but with Hirzel and others, <hi type="italic">assutores mendacii,</hi> such as patch on lies, i.e., charge falsely, since they desire throughout to make him out to be a sinner punished according to his desert. This explanation is also confirmed by Job 14:17. Another explanation is given by Hupfeld: <hi type="italic">sarcinatores false </hi>= <hi type="italic">inanes, inutiles</hi>, so that שׁקר signifies what lies = what deceives, as in the parallel member of the verse אלל,<note placement="foot">In the Talmudic, the jugular vein, the cutting of which produces death, is called אלל (later עצב, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ṣb</hi>), according to which (<hi type="italic">b. Chullin</hi> 121a) it is explained: healer of the jugular artery, i.e., those who try to heal what is incurable, therefore charlatans, - a strange idea, which has arisen from the defective form of writing אלל. The lxx translates ἰαταὶ κακῶν.</note> nothingness, and also עמל (<reference osisRef="Job.16.2">Job 16:2</reference>) in a similar connection, is not an objective but attributive genitive; but <reference osisRef="Ps.119.69">Psa 119:69</reference> is decisive against this interpretation of שׁקר טפלי. The parallelism is not so exactly adjusted, as e.g., even רפאי does not on account of the parallel with טפלי signify patchers, ῥάπται, but: they are not able to heal Job’s wounds with the medicine of consolation; they are <hi type="italic">medici nihili</hi>, useless physicians. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.28">Pro 17:28</reference>, “Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise,” applies to them, <hi type="italic">si tacuisses, sapiens mansisses;</hi> or, as a rabbinical proverb of similar meaning, quoted by Heidenheim, says, השׂגה בהשׂגה הלאות, “the fatigue of comprehension is comprehension,” i.e., the silent pause before a problem is half the solution. The jussive form וּתהי, it would be (Ges. §128, 2), is used in the conclusion of the wish. Thus he challenges them to hear his תּוכחת (תּוכחה) and his רבוה. Hirzel is quite right when he says the former does not mean defence (justification), nor the latter proofs (counter-evidence); תוכחת is, according to his signification (<hi type="italic">significatus</hi>, in distinction from sensus), ἔλεγχος, <hi type="italic">correptio</hi> (lxx, Vulg.), and here not so much refutation and answer, as correction in an ethical sense, in correspondence with which רבות is also intended of reproaches, reproofs, or reprimands.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.13.7-Job.11.7">Job 13:7-11   7</reference>  Will ye speak what is wrong for God, <div eID="gen7356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7357" type="x-p"/> And speak what is deceitful for Him?   8  Will ye be partial for Him, <div eID="gen7357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7358" type="x-p"/> Or will ye play the part of God’s advocates?   9  Would it be pleasant if He should search you out, <div eID="gen7358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7359" type="x-p"/> Or can ye jest with Him, as one jesteth with men? 10  He will surely expose you <div eID="gen7359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7360" type="x-p"/> If ye secretly act with partiality. 11  Will not His majesty confound you, <div eID="gen7360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7361" type="x-p"/> And His fear fall upon you? <div eID="gen7361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7362" type="x-p"/> Their advocacy of God - this is the thought of this strophe - is an injustice to Job, and an evil service rendered to God, which cannot escape undisguised punishment from Him. They set themselves up as God’s advocates (לאל ריב, like לבּעל ריב, Jdg 6:31), and at the same time accept His person, <hi type="italic">accipiunt</hi> (as in <hi type="italic">acceptus</hi> = <hi type="italic">gratus</hi>), or lift it up, i.e., favour, or give preference to, His person, viz., at the expense of the truth: they are partial in His favour, as they are twice reminded and given to understand by the <hi type="italic">fut. energicum</hi> תּשּׂאוּן. The addition of בּסּתר (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.10">Job 13:10</reference></hi>) implies that they conceal their better knowledge by the assumption of an earnest tone and bearing, expressive of the strongest conviction that they are in the right. They know that Job is not a flagrant sinner; nevertheless they deceive themselves with the idea that he is, and by reason of this delusion they take up the cause of God against him. Such perversion of the truth <hi type="italic">in majorem Dei gloriam</hi> is an abomination to God. When He searches them, His advocates, out (חקר, as Prov.Job 28:11), they will become conscious of it; or will God be mocked, as one mocketh mortal men? Comp. <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Gal 6:7</reference> for a similar thought. חתל is <hi type="italic">inf. absol. </hi>after the form תּללּ, and תּהתלּוּ is also to be derived from תּללּ, and is <hi type="italic">fut. Hiph.,</hi> the preformative not being syncopated, for תּתלּוּ (Ges. §53, rem. 7); not <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, from התל (as 1Ki 18:27), with the doubling of the middle radical resolved (Olsh. in his <hi type="italic">Lehrb</hi>. S. 577). God is not pleased with λατρεία (Joh 16:2) which gives the honour to Him, but not to truth, such ζῆλος Θεοῦ ἀλλ ̓ ου ̓ κατ ̓ ἐπίγνωσιν (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">Rom 10:2</reference>), such advocacy contrary to one’s better knowledge and conscience, in which the end is thought to sanctify the means. Such advocacy must be put to shame and confounded when He who needs no concealment of the truth for His justification is manifest in His שׂאת, i.e., not: in the kindling of His wrath (after Jdg 20:38; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>), but: in His exaltation (correctly by Ralbag: התנשׂאותו ורוממותו), and by His direct influence brings all untruth to light. It is the boldest thought imaginable, that one dare not have respect even to the person of God when one is obliged to lie to one’s self. And still it is also self-evident. For God and truth can never be antagonistic.

entries.content_osis: Job 13:17-19 17  Hear, O hear my confession, <div eID="gen7376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7377" type="x-p"/> And let my declaration echo in your ears. 18  Behold now! I have arranged the cause, <div eID="gen7377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7378" type="x-p"/> I know that I shall maintain the right. 19  Who then can contend with me? <div eID="gen7378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7379" type="x-p"/> Then, indeed, I would be silent and expire. <div eID="gen7379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7380" type="x-p"/> Eager for the accomplishment of his wish that he might himself take his cause before God, and as though in imagination it were so, he invites the friends to be present to hear his defence of himself. מלּה (in Arabic directly used for confession = religion) is the confession which he will lay down, and אחוה the declaration that he will make in evidence, i.e., the proof of his innocence. On עתּה כּי (in meaning not different to אז כּי), vid., <reference osisRef="Job.3.13">Job 3:13</reference>; Job 8:6. In <reference osisRef="Job.13.19">Job 13:19</reference> that is granted as possible which, according to the declaration of his conscience, Job must consider as absolutely impossible. Therefore he clings to the desire of being able to bring his cause before God, and becomes more and more absorbed in the thought.

entries.content_osis: Job 13:20-22 20  Only two things do not unto me, <div eID="gen7380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7381" type="x-p"/> Then will I not hide myself from Thy countenance: 21  Withdraw Thy hand from me, <div eID="gen7381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7382" type="x-p"/> And let Thy fear not terrify me - 22  Call then and I will answer, <div eID="gen7382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7383" type="x-p"/> Or I will speak and answer Thou me! <div eID="gen7383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7384" type="x-p"/> He makes only two conditions in his prayer, as he has already expressed it in <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference> : (<reference osisRef="Job.9.1">1</reference>) That God would grant him a cessation of his troubles; (2) That He would not overwhelm him with His majesty. The chastening hand of God is generally called יד elsewhere; but in spite of this prevalent usage of the language, כּף cannot be understood here (comp. on the contrary <reference osisRef="Job.33.7">Job 33:7</reference>) otherwise than of the hand (<reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference> : the rod) of God, which lies heavily on Job. The painful pressure of that hand would prevent the collecting and ordering of his thoughts required for meeting with God, and the אימה (Codd. defectively אמתך) of God would completely crush and confound him. But if God grants these two things: to remove His hand for a time, and not to turn the terrible side of His majesty to him, then he is ready whether God should himself open the cause or permit him to have the first word. Correctly Mercerus: <hi type="italic">optionem ei dat ut aut actoris aut rei personam deligat, sua fretus innocentia, sed interim sui oblitus et immodicus.</hi> In contrast with God he feels himself to be a poor worm, but his consciousness of innocence makes him a Titan. <div eID="gen7384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7385" type="x-p"/> He now says what he would ask God; or rather, he now asks Him, since he vividly pictures to himself the action with God which he desires. His imagination anticipates the reality of that which is longed for. Modern expositors begin a new division at Job 13:23. But Job’s speech does not yet take a new turn; it goes on further continually <hi type="italic">uno tenore</hi>.

entries.content_osis: Job 13:23-25 23  How many are mine iniquities and sins? <div eID="gen7385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7386" type="x-p"/> Make me to know my transgression and sin! -  - 24  Wherefore dost Thou hide Thy face, <div eID="gen7386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7387" type="x-p"/> And regard me as Thine enemy? 25  Wilt Thou frighten away a leaf driven to and fro, <div eID="gen7387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7388" type="x-p"/> And pursue the dry stubble? <div eID="gen7388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7389" type="x-p"/> When עון and חטּאת, פּשׁע and חטּאת, are used in close connection, the latter, which describes sin as failing and error, signifies sins of weakness (infirmities, <hi type="italic">Schwachheitssünde</hi>); whereas עון (prop. distorting or bending) signifies misdeed, and פשׁע (prop. breaking loose, or away from, Arab. <hi type="italic">fsq</hi>) wickedness which designedly estranges itself from God and removes from favour, both therefore malignant sin (<hi type="italic">Bosheitssünde</hi>).<note placement="foot">Comp. the development of the idea of the synonyms for sin in von Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Schriftbeweis</hi>, i. 483ff., at the commencement of the fourth <hi type="italic">Lehrstück</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen7389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7390" type="x-p"/> The bold self-confidence which is expressed in the question and challenge of <reference osisRef="Job.13.23">Job 13:23</reference> is, in <reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference>, changed to grievous astonishment that God does not appear to him, and on the contrary continues to pursue him as an enemy without investigating his cause. When עון and חטּאת, פּשׁע and חטּאת, are used in close connection, the latter, which describes sin as failing and error, signifies sins of weakness (infirmities, Schwachheitssünde ); whereas עון (prop. distorting or bending) signifies misdeed, and פשׁע (prop. breaking loose, or away from, Arab. fsq ) wickedness which designedly estranges itself from God and removes from favour, both therefore malignant sin ( Bosheitssünde ). Comp. the development of the idea of the synonyms for sin in von Hofmann, Schriftbeweis , i. 483ff., at the commencement of the fourth Lehrstück . The bold self-confidence which is expressed in the question and challenge of Job 13:23 is, in Job 13:24 , changed to grievous astonishment that God does not appear to him, and on the contrary continues to pursue him as an enemy without investigating his cause. Has the Almighty then pleasure in scaring away a leaf that is already blown to and fro? העלה, with He interrog., like החכם, Job 15:2 , according to Ges. §100, 4. ערץ used as transitive here, like Psa 10:18 , to terrify, scare away affrighted. Does it give Him satisfaction to pursue dried-up stubble? By את (before an indeterminate noun, according to Ges. §117, 2) he points δεικτικῶς to himself: he, the powerless one, completely deprived of strength by sickness and pain, is as dried-up stubble; nevertheless God is after him, as though He would get rid of every trace of a dangerous enemy by summoning His utmost strength against him.

entries.content_osis: Job 13:26-28 26  For Thou decreest bitter things against me, <div eID="gen7390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7391" type="x-p"/> And causest me to possess the iniquities of my youth, 27  And puttest my feet in the stocks, <div eID="gen7391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7392" type="x-p"/> And observest all my ways. <div eID="gen7392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7393" type="x-p"/> Thou makest for thyself a circle round the soles of my feet, 28  Round one who moulders away as worm-eaten, <div eID="gen7393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> As a garment that the moth gnaweth. <div eID="gen7394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7395" type="x-p"/> He is conscious of having often prayed: “Remember not the sins of my youth, and my transgressions: according to Thy mercy remember Thou me,” <reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">Psa 25:7</reference>; and still he can only regard his affliction as the inheritance (i.e., entailed upon him by sins not repented of) of the sins of his youth, since he has no sins of his mature years that would incur wrath, to reproach himself with. He does not know how to reconcile with the justice of God the fact that He again records against him sins, the forgiveness of which he implores soon after their commission, and decrees (כּתב, as <reference osisRef="Ps.149.9">Psa 149:9</reference>, and as used elsewhere in the book of Job with reference to the recording of judgment) for him on account of them such bitter punishment (מררות, <hi type="italic">amara</hi>, bitter calamities; comp. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">Deu 32:32</reference>, “bitter” grapes). And the two could not indeed be harmonized, if it really were thus. So long as a man remains an object of the divine mercy, his sins that have been once forgiven are no more the object of divine judgment. But Job can understand his affliction only as an additional punishment. The conflict of temptation through which he is passing has made God’s loving-kindness obscure to him. He appears to himself to be like a prisoner whose feet are forced into the holes of a סד, i.e., the block or log of wood in which the feet of a criminal are fastened, and which he must shuffle about with him when he moves; perhaps connected with Arab. <hi type="italic">sadda , occludere, opplere</hi> (<hi type="italic">foramen</hi>), elsewhere מהפּכת (from the forcible twisting or fastening), Chald. סדיא, סדנא, Syr. <hi type="italic">sado ,</hi> by which <reference osisRef="Acts.16.24">Act 16:24</reference>, ξύλον = ποδοκάκη, is rendered; Lat. <hi type="italic">cippus</hi> (which Ralbag compares), <hi type="italic">codex</hi> (in Plautus an instrument of punishment for slaves), or also <hi type="italic">nervus</hi>. The verb תּשׂם which belongs to it, and is found also in <reference osisRef="Job.33.11">Job 33:11</reference> in the same connection, is of the jussive form, but is neither jussive nor optative in meaning, as also the future with shortened vowel (e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.27.22">Job 27:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.19">Job 40:19</reference>) or apocopated (<reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>) is used elsewhere from the preference of poetry for a short pregnant form. He seems to himself like a criminal whose steps are closely watched (שׁמר, as <reference osisRef="Job.10.14">Job 10:14</reference>), in order that he may not have the undeserved enjoyment of freedom, and may not avoid the execution for which he is reserved by effecting an escape by flight. Instead of ארחתי, the reading adopted by Ben-Ascher, Ben-Naphtali writes ארחתי, with <hi type="italic">Cholem</hi> in the first syllable; both modes of punctuation change without any fixed law also in other respects in the inflexion of ארח, as of ארחה, a caravan, the construct is both ארחות, <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job 6:19</reference>, and ארחות. It is scarcely necessary to remark that the verbs in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.13.27">Job 13:27</reference></hi> are addressed to God, and are not intended as the <hi type="italic">third pers. fem.</hi> in reference to the stocks (Ralbag). The roots of the feet are undoubtedly their undermost parts, therefore the soles. But what is the meaning of תּתחקּה? The Vulg., Syr., and Parchon explain: Thou fixest thine attention upon ... , but certainly according to mere conjecture; Ewald, by the help of the Arabic <hi type="italic">tahhakkaka ala</hi>: Thou securest thyself ... , but there is not the least necessity to depart from the ordinary use of the word, as those also do who explain: Thou makest a law or boundary (Aben-Ezra, Ges., Hahn, Schlottm.). The verb חקה is the usual word (certainly cognate and interchangeable with חקק) for carved-out work (intaglio), and perhaps with colour rubbed in, or filled up with metal (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.14">Eze 23:14</reference>); it signifies to hew into, to carve, to dig a trench. Stickel is in some measure true to this meaning when he explains: Thou scratchest, pressest (producing blood); by which rendering, however, the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. is not duly recognised. Raschi is better, <hi type="italic">tu t'affiches</hi>, according to which Mercerus: <hi type="italic">velut affixus vestigiis pedum meorum adhaeres, ne quâ elabi possim aut effugere. </hi> But a closer connection with the ordinary use of the word is possible. Accordingly Rosenm., Umbreit, and others render: Thou markest a line round my feet (drawest a circle round); Hirz., however, in the strictest sense of the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>.: Thou diggest thyself in (layest thyself as a circular line about my feet). But the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. does not necessarily mean <hi type="italic">se insculpere</hi>, but, as התפשׁט <hi type="italic">sibi exuere,</hi> התפתח <hi type="italic">sibi solvere,</hi> התחנן <hi type="italic">sibi propitium facere,</hi> it may also mean sibi insculpere, which does not give so strange a representation: Thou makest to thyself furrows (or also: lines) round the soles of my feet, so that they cannot move beyond the narrow boundaries marked out by thee. With והוּא, <reference osisRef="Job.13.28">Job 13:28</reference>, a circumstantial clause begins: While he whom Thou thus fastenest in as a criminal, etc. Observe the fine rhythmical accentuation <hi type="italic">achālo ‛asch</hi>. Since God whom he calls upon does not appear, Job’s defiance is changed to timidity. The elegiac tone, into which his bold tone has passed, is continued in Job 14.  <chapter eID="Job.13"/> <div eID="gen7395" type="x-p"/>
